item.title: Office Buildings at 48 Cents, Family Office Says Wonderful
item.description: A fifth of office loans are underwater. Ruh is offering forty-eight cents and expects a yes.

item.title: Let Your Driver Worry About The Pump
item.description: Diesel is up 64 percent. The man in the back seat has a driver for that.

item.title: Shoppers Pay More for the Same Cereal, Call It an Upgrade
item.description: The box got smaller and the price went up. Shoppers call the new one an upgrade.

item.title: Machines That Cost a Country's GDP Still Can't Book a Table
item.description: $106 billion in a quarter. It still can't get a table at eight.

item.title: Insuring a Roof Now Costs More Than the Handbag It Protects
item.description: The state pool raised rates 29.1 percent. Ray's premium is $5,800.

item.title: Bank Airs Ad of Couple Celebrating They Can Afford the Minimum
item.description: Thirteen percent of balances are ninety days late. The couple in the ad can afford the minimum.

item.title: Health Firm Loses $66 Million Serving People Who Can't Pay More
item.description: A company built on affordable healthcare reports record subscribers and a widening loss, because every patient it helps on the cheap tier costs it money. The mission is working. The numbers agree it is working.

item.title: Cirrus Buys Back Shares Its Refounding Founder Keeps Selling, Both Sides Pleased
item.description: The software company laid off 7 percent of its staff in October, costing up to $75 million. Over the same year, it has bought back nearly $1 billion of its shares.

item.title: Summit Spends $4 Billion on Exits, Counts It as $6 Billion in Savings
item.description: The newly merged media giant plans to cut $2.2 billion by flattening management layers and shrinking office footprints. It also mandated five-day in-office attendance.

item.title: Automaker Searches Pockets, Discovers Wage Money After All
item.description: The auto-parts supplier told its union it could not afford their demands. The same week it started permanent layoffs, its board approved a $60 million stock buyback and a record $46 million dividend.

item.title: Telecom Confident Its Own Shares Are Worth $19.45, No, Really, They Are
item.description: When the bidder's own stock at its own closing price is used to calculate the offer's value, and the market says the math is wrong, finance says the market is wrong.

item.title: $298 Million Refund Cashed by the Same People That Raised the Price
item.description: A company that blamed tariffs for jacking up prices gets the money back and routes it straight to the C-suite, because the machine doesn't correct itself.

item.title: Fuel That Hauled the 2x4 to the Site Now Costs More Than the 2x4
item.description: The man building $3M condos is furious that a 2x4 costs eight bucks, and he is saying this while standing in a bathroom that costs more than a house.

item.title: Post Office Makes Its Temporary Surcharge Permanent, Then Adds More
item.description: The agency has clarified that 'temporary' refers to the period during which the charge is being collected, not the charge itself.

item.title: Landlord Cheers Tax Increase That His Tenants Will Pay
item.description: The man who owns forty units on Reading Road has never been happier about a piece of paper that will cost him money.

item.title: Footwear Hits Record High as Man Buys Fifth Pair of Identical Sneakers
item.description: He is on his fifth pair of the same shoe and cannot fathom why anyone would complain about a price that has barely moved since the Obama administration.

item.title: One Spark Plug Costs More Than the Lobster Dinner the CEO Ate Last Night
item.description: The man who has never changed a tire in his life is suddenly an expert on internal combustion economics.

item.title: Son's Toy Car Beats Father's Hedge Fund for the Month
item.description: At the birthday party, he did the math on a die-cast car and now nobody can get him off the patio.

item.title: Greenwich Motivated Seller Who Has Carried Two Mortgages for 14 Months Begins Accepting Applications for the Role of Buyer
item.description: Existing home sales hit a 16-year low of 3.75 million annualized in October. Every price tier declined, including the $1-million-and-up segment. In Greenwich, Connecticut, a Colonial has been on the market for 14 months.

item.title: Thornwood Partners Frames Negative Real Wages as a Loyalty Discount, Advises Employees to Consider It a Character-Building Opportunity
item.description: Real wages have been negative for seven consecutive months. Wages rose 3.1% year-over-year; inflation ran at approximately 4%. Thornwood Partners has reframed the gap as a voluntary contribution.

item.title: Fed Chair Assumes Commuters Helicopter to Work, Blames Bus Fare Hike on Increased Rotor Maintenance
item.description: Intracity transit fares rose 6.6% in a single month — the largest monthly increase since 2020, annualized to over 100%. The Federal Reserve attributes the spike to rising rotor-maintenance costs.

item.title: Verde Family Office Declares Romaine Lettuce a Veblen Good, Advises Clients to Serve It on Velvet
item.description: Romaine lettuce hit $3.49 a pound, up 7.3% in one month — now more expensive per pound than chicken. Verde Family Office says the price is the point.

item.title: Ashford Capital Points to the Chicken Price on Your Receipt, Hails Tyson's $1M Profit on $14.6B as Operational Excellence
item.description: Tyson Foods reported $1 million in operating income on $14.585 billion in revenue — a margin of 0.0068%. The company posted a net loss of $74 million. Its beef segment lost $514 million. Ashford Capital's Harold Pender called it a victory lap.

item.title: Brackenridge Family Office Advises Formula-Fed Infants to Trade Up to the Premium Tier
item.description: Basic formula rose 5.1% in a single month — the largest increase since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the category in 1997. Brackenridge Family Office sees a generational buying opportunity.

item.title: The Men Who've Failed To Beat The S&P For 14 Years Are Confident The Market Will Finally Notice How Wrong They Were
item.description: The industry's longest winless streak continued, with managers describing their stewardship as prematurely correct and the outflows as a tax on patience.

item.title: Art Built His Office Park In 2004. A Family Office; Bought It In 2026, Explaining The Economy Needs Parking More Than Art
item.description: Wealthy families now fund forced sales at a discount, a role regulators described as inevitable and sellers described as generous, eventually.

item.title: Keisha's $6.87 Coffee Cost $41.87 Because The Bank Processes Happier Numbers Before Sadder Ones
item.description: Revenue rose 9.4% to a four-year high as lenders attributed the bonanza to a chronic shortage of balance on the part of account holders.

item.title: Company Hires Darren, Reclassifies Darren, Absorbs Darren, And Invites Darren To Apply Again As Darren
item.description: Employers confirmed they would love to bring somebody on board, but the job keeps evolving out from under the handshake into a position that no longer exists, and then out from under that.

item.title: Algorithm That Replaced Its Traders Decides It Also Wants To Fire Them A Second Time For Dramatic Effect
item.description: The model priced the data, revised the forecast, and then chose to spend the remainder of the session deleting the traders who had the meeting.

item.title: The 617,000 Laid Off This Year Were Named Raymond, A Call Most Of Them Answered With Earning Ceased
item.description: Net job cuts slowed 44% from last year's total, a statistic that confused only the recently separated, who could not see it from where they landed.

item.title: Treasury Selloff Accelerates as Bond Market Learns the Worst Part of Being Right Is Having Been Right the Whole Time
item.description: With the 10-year toward 5.1% and hawkish Fed bets rising, the long end reports that vindication, apparently, hurts.

item.title: Card Issuers Raise Limits on Customers Already in Debt, Explain Strategy as 'Giving the Rope Time to Work'
item.description: With balances and minimums climbing, lenders say the best defense against default is a higher ceiling.

item.title: Banks Believe in AI So Hard They Will Not Give It a Single Dollar, a Position They Describe as Principled
item.description: Lenders are again wary of financing data-center debt, describing their confidence in AI as personal and their confidence in its invoices as contractual.

item.title: PCE Hits 3.6%, White House Notes Number Is Down if You Only Count Things in Someone Else's Cart
item.description: As inflation stays above target, officials note the figure is down only if you look at the goods people used to buy.

item.title: Fed Worried the Labor Market Has Gotten Too Settled to Count Anyone As Working
item.description: Federal Reserve officials are worried the labor market has gotten so settled that a person can no longer be counted as hired, laid off, or doing anything at all.

item.title: Thames National Profit Jumps 12% As Bank Proves Algebra Where 5,000 Fewer People Equal More Money
item.description: The bank says machine learning will remove 5% of its workforce while profits climb, a pairing it describes as the new healthy.

item.title: As Mortgage Rates Climb, Finance Industry Clarifies That a Roof Is Not Actually Housing Unless You Have a Second One
item.description: With ownership unaffordable for five million more Americans, lenders confirm rent is the answer and is not, technically, housing.

item.title: Thomson Reuters Announces $500M Buyback, Controlling Owner Graciously Sells Shares to the One Person Who Already Owned Them
item.description: The company's controlling investor will participate proportionally in the buyback, graciously accepting the shares it already controls back.

item.title: European Banks Beat Profit Estimates, Celebrate By Buying Back Exactly As Much Of Themselves As They Can Before Anyone Asks Where It Came From
item.description: UBS and BNP Paribas delivered strong quarters and accelerated buybacks, resolving the eternal question of what to do with gains.

item.title: Keystone Bank Calls AI-Driven Layoffs 'Attrition As Our Friend,' Reaffirms That Nothing Has Ever Valued The Company As Much As Leaving
item.description: The bank plans to shrink its workforce by allowing AI to do what dentures could not, and management says it has only this one friend.
